rv.q: Meticulously off-handed, it’s funny and sad, a performance to be savored in a totally engaging little triumph of a show.

Mark Rylance is once again ruling audiences at the Belasco Theater, where the strangely enchanting “Farinelli and the King,” Claire van Kampen’s shimmering fairy tale for grown-ups, opened on Sunday night.
Watching Rylance convey the pain, fear and vulnerability of that striving is heart-rending and unforgettable.

Mark Rylance as King Philip V and Sam Crane as Farinelli in "Farinelli and the King." Credit: Simon Annand WHERE Belasco Theatre, 111 W. 44th St., Manhattan INFO $32-$169, 212-239-6200, telecharge.com BOTTOM LINE Glorious music and Mark Rylance. King Philip V of Spain is certifiable, of that there’s no doubt.
Like you do if you are Rylance, who dives deep inside wacky Philippe in a performance as empathetic as it is seemingly spontaneous.

There's not much to Claire van Kampen's simplistic script for 'Farinelli and the King,' the play now running on Broadway after premiering at Shakespeare's Globe in London. But with a lead performance by Oscar and Tony winner Mark Rylance in full sail, it's enough.
The result is a show that is all frosting and no cake.

Unlike in Alan Bennett’s play The Madness of George III, and its film adaptation, the deteriorating mental health of a monarch here doesn’t constitute a sustaining narrative arc, even if Rylance’s commanding performance remains the center of attention.
The pleasures of John Dove's production—the music, Rylance's halting propulsion, Jonathan Fensom's sumptuous sets and costumes—gleam to no purpose, real jewels glued to a trinket crown.
Mark Rylance is unparalleled as an actor.
Rylance gives a full-bodied and endearing performance that combines volatile behavior and over-the-top comedy with gentle contemplation.
Fans of trained actors filling Broadway houses with the richness of their unamplified voices (not to mention those who believe electric lights are overrated) have reason to rejoice.
English playwright Claire van Kampen’s fact-based but liberally embroidered drama isn’t so sensational — and can't get past one obstacle.
Whatever, your eyes and ears will leave Farinelli happy indeed.
After the king exits for good, only the superb music can keep the audience awake.
Van Kampen’s disjointed storytelling and John Dove’s pedestrian direction, however, turn it into something nearer soap opera — but without either the intrigue or the sex of that lesser genre.

But for the performance of Rylance, who is as always remarkable, and Davies, who is a delicious surprise and deserving of the two final bows that Rylance engineers, Farinelli and The King remains a tedious bit of business.
Rylance, one of the greatest English stage actors, inhabits the character. To see him is thrilling.

cn.t: Rylance delivers a masterful performance that elevates van Kampen's thin, simplistic script about an 18th-century mad king soothed by a castrato's voice. Critics praise the glorious music and candlelit staging, but note the plot lacks depth.

sg.ra: Belasco was designed by David Belasco as a 'living room' with a shallow depth to support the Little Theater movement's emphasis on actor-audience proximity. Center Orchestra rows B-D sit at the ideal distance (reviewers cite row B as the fourth row from stage at 'perfect distance') with head-on actor views. Mezzanine overhang begins at row J per SeatPlan, so rows BB-H stay clear.

SeatPlan confirms 'The Mezzanine overhang begins at row J, meaning seats behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Rows J-Q trade top-of-stage visibility for lower prices. Headout and TickPick both flag G-P/F-O center as value picks. Row N's extra legroom offsets the overhang compromise for tall patrons.

SeatPlan: 'Seats at the Left and Right edges suffer from restricted views of the stage,' particularly corner seats in rows B-E. TickPick confirms 'Far Left/Right Orchestra: Angled views may occur.' Historic box configuration and shallow house geometry amplify side-angle distortion.

sg.vl: Aerial sweet spot, skip row A
sg.ra: Mezzanine hangs close and center row C delivers aerial perspective with decent rake. Row A is a common trap: 'Mezzanine row A seat 111 was obstructed view, and the rail literally blocks half of the stage' (Tripadvisor user report). Balcony overhang begins at mezz row C per SeatPlan, so rows A-B stay open-topped but row A's safety bar offsets that benefit.

Headout flags F-H center as the mezzanine value range. Balcony overhang starting at row C means rows E-H sit under it — top of set may be cut. Side mezzanine suffers progressively more restricted angles 'due to stage curvature' (SeatPlan). Acceptable for dialogue-heavy work but not flown spectacle.

Center Balcony 'extends back six rows on a steep rake which provides a bird's-eye-view of the stage' (SeatPlan). Rows B-D balance price and sightline. Distance is the honest tradeoff: AVFMS reviewer on Maybe Happy Ending noted 'the real problem is how far back the balcony is. You'll have to lean forward to see for most of the show.' Row A safety rail can also obstruct.

sg.vl: Up to 1/3 of stage cut off
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'the curve of the section and other features including the Left Boxes may cut off up to a third of the stage at the outside.' Combined with steep rake, distance, and row A rail, side balcony is the worst seat class in the house. Historic 1907 box architecture is the root cause — it cannot be engineered out per production.
